clue.text: Flier on city border recalled by relative

parts.note: RE is the Latin-derived 'on the matter of', as in a memo heading
a father is a close relative

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the city and border words are brought back in reverse order

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
a rim is an edge or border

explanation.surface: Someone flying in over the edge of a city is met by a family member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot or passenger, but it is the butterfly. Only the city and border pair turn round; the first two pieces read forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: This common orange-and-black butterfly flies, so a crossword can call any butterfly a flier.

clue.text: Dodgy scheme run with lots of dosh papa's left

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: if papa has left, the letter for papa has gone from the word

parts.note: a packet is informal British for a large sum of money; dosh is slang for cash
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A father has walked out after running a shady scheme that made him a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: PACKET loses its P and R goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a dishonest moneymaking operation, so it means a fraudulent or shady scheme.

clue.text: Dame tackling centre of staircase that's steep

indicators.note: to tackle someone is to get hold of them, so the dame's name grips the letter

parts.note: Dame Judi Dench is a famous British actress

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, here the fifth of nine

parts.note: the middle letter

explanation.surface: An elderly dame struggles to climb a staircase that is very steep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steep' looks like an adjective for the stairs but it is the verb soak. R goes inside DENCH.
explanation.definitionFit: To steep something is to soak it thoroughly in liquid, which is what drench means as a verb.

clue.text: Regret sauce being infused by juice and cream

indicators.note: a liquid infused into something soaks into it, so one word ends up inside the other

parts.note: a dip is a thick sauce for dipping food into
sap is the juice of a plant
an ointment is a medicinal cream

explanation.surface: A cook regrets a sauce flavoured with fruit juice and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Disappointment is sorrow at hopes not met, so it fits regret as a noun for that feeling.

clue.text: Swear when meat price changes

indicators.note: when something changes it is altered, so these letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper curses when the butcher puts the cost of meat up.
explanation.definitionFit: To imprecate is to utter curses, a formal word for swearing at someone or calling down evil.

clue.text: Rich tapestry vulgar rascal frames

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the outer words surround the letters wanted

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of vulgar and the start of rascal

explanation.surface: A crude scoundrel has an expensive wall hanging framed.
explanation.definitionFit: An arras is a richly woven wall hanging named after the French town Arras, famed for such tapestry.

clue.text: Serves sides female leaves

indicators.note: when something leaves it goes away, so the letter for female is dropped

parts.note: the faces of a solid are its sides
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman walks off a court after her serves keep hitting the sidelines.
explanation.walkthrough: FACES loses its F to leave ACES.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis an ace is a serve the receiver cannot touch, so aces are a kind of serves.

clue.text: Call contractors about small glasses

parts.note: to cry is to call out

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the muscle word runs backwards

parts.note: lats are the large back muscles, and muscles work by contracting
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone phones builders about some little drinking glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contractors' suggests builders; here they are muscles, which contract.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal is fine glassware, so crystals are drinking vessels made of it, that is good glasses.

clue.text: Sly northern cove misrepresented ability to pay bills

indicators.note: something misrepresented is given in a false form, so the letters are set out wrongly

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for northern
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cunning northern fellow lied about whether he could cover his debts.
explanation.walkthrough: Cove is old British slang for a man, which steers the reader away from the bay.
explanation.definitionFit: Solvency is the financial state of having enough money or assets to meet all debts as they fall due.

clue.text: Respite from engineers drilling poolside?

indicators.note: a drill bores into something, so the engineers go inside the other phrase

parts.note: a poolside is an area for bathing; the question mark flags a whimsical description
RE is the Royal Engineers of the British Army

explanation.surface: Workmen are drilling by the swimming pool, and you need a break from them.
explanation.walkthrough: RE goes after the B of BATHING SPACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A breathing space is a short pause that lets you recover, which is exactly a respite.

clue.text: Musical in disorder when child plays part of Mike

indicators.note: the child takes over the role played by Mike, standing in for it

parts.note: a mess is a state of disorder
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A stage show falls into chaos when a child actor takes on a role.
explanation.walkthrough: In MESS, 'plays part of' puts CH (child) in the place of M (Mike). Chess is the 1980s musical by Tim Rice with Benny and Björn of ABBA.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is the title of a West End and Broadway stage show with songs such as One Night in Bangkok.

clue.text: Entrance accommodates fish depiction

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to house them inside, so one word holds another

parts.note: a portal is a doorway or entrance
a ray is a flat sea fish

explanation.surface: A grand doorway has a fish carved into it as a decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrayal is a representation of someone in art or acting, which is what a depiction is.

clue.text: One that's flown in 112.5 degrees crossing coast?

indicators.note: the bearing is split and straddles the other word, lying across it on both sides

parts.note: east-south-east is the compass bearing of 112.5 degrees
a cape is a headland on a coast; the question mark admits it is an example

explanation.surface: A bird flying on a bearing of 112.5 degrees passes over the shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: The bearing splits after its second letter to go round the headland. 'Flown' here means fled, not travelled by air.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly can mean to flee or run away, and an escapee is someone who has fled captivity.

clue.text: Young actress ultimately internalised shock

indicators.note: the young actress's ultimate letter is internalised: taken off the end of her word and tucked back inside it, two places in

parts.note: a starlet is a young actress hoping to become a star

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming actress has been quietly carrying a shock inside her.
explanation.walkthrough: The young actress's last letter does not vanish: 'internalised' moves it from the end into the middle, so the word is rebuilt rather than shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: To startle someone is to shock or alarm them suddenly.

clue.text: New local inn hooch largely unfit for purpose?

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters that follow are put into a fresh order
largely means most of it, so the word hooch loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A new local pub sells home-made liquor that is not fit to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like part of the pub's description but is the anagram signal: LOCAL, INN and HOOC (hooch 'largely') are mixed together. The question mark flags the joke that an alcohol-free drink is useless for getting drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Playfully, a drink containing no alcohol fails at the job a boozer wants from it, so it is useless for that aim.

clue.text: Bit cross carrying case of rare liqueur

parts.note: a bit is an old word for a small coin, as in a threepenny bit

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so the cross word holds those letters inside

parts.note: a tau cross is T-shaped, named after the Greek letter

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so the first and last letters of rare are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: An irritable man carries a crate of an unusual drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry; it is the T-shaped cross named after a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cointreau is a French orange-flavoured spirit, a branded example of a sweet liqueur.

clue.text: Sober under tree? This might get you plastered

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part placed under another follows it in the grid

parts.note: a fir is a conifer
staid means sober and serious

explanation.surface: A man sitting soberly under a tree wonders what drink might get him drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' suggests drunk, especially after 'sober'; here it means covered with a sticking plaster, the British word for an adhesive bandage.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatment for a cut often ends with a sticking plaster, so emergency medical help can leave you bandaged.

clue.text: Guard first-class bottle of plonk?

parts.note: screw is British slang for a prison officer
top means best, first-rate

explanation.surface: A security guard gets a top-quality bottle of cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, which usually comes in a bottle with a twist cap rather than a cork.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap wine bottles are commonly sealed with a twist cap, so the container itself gets that name.

clue.text: Troublesome pigeons regularly stopping where sisters stay

indicators.note: to stop a hole is to plug it, so these letters sit inside the other phrase

parts.note: nuns, called sisters, live in a convent

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the bird word is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Pigeons keep getting into the nunnery and causing a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: IEN goes into IN CONVENT between CONVEN and T.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inconvenient causes difficulty or bother, so it is troublesome in the mild everyday sense.

clue.text: Male in second part of play sealed envelope

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second

indicators.note: in places the male inside the theatre word

parts.note: an act is a section of a play
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man in the second act of a drama seals an envelope on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachet is a small closed packet holding sugar, shampoo or the like, so it is a little sealed pouch.

clue.text: Watch from China worn by half of troops

indicators.note: something worn by a person is around them, so the friend word goes round the letters

parts.note: china is cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate), and a mate is a pal

indicators.note: taking half of a six-letter word drops its last three letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A watch made in China is worn by half the soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' and 'worn' suggest a wristwatch; it is guard duty. China is not the country but cockney rhyming slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A patrol is a group keeping guard by moving round an area, so it is a watch in the sentry sense.

clue.text: Side very exposed on back of this vessel

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only the last letter of the word this is kept

parts.note: the final letter
a side is a sports team

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters of very are peeled away

parts.note: the inner letters with the outer pair removed

explanation.surface: One side of a ship is left dangerously open at the stern.
explanation.walkthrough: TEAM and ER are placed on S, with S coming first.
explanation.definitionFit: A steamer is a ship driven by steam power, so it is a type of seagoing vessel.

clue.text: Brahmin periodically working around capital?

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter of the priest word is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

indicators.note: turned around, the word for working faces the other way

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A Hindu priest is working his way round a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for money, and capital is money too; the question mark admits the slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital is wealth or funds, and rhino is a dated British slang word for cash.

clue.text: Dish encased by twisted lead at Sotheby's

indicators.note: twisted round, the letter string is read from right to left
something encased is held inside a casing, so the letters lie within the run of words

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of lead, all of at, and the start of Sotheby's

explanation.surface: An item is sold at a famous auction house, wrapped up in twisted lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards, the run inside the phrase spells TOSTADA. Sotheby's is a London auction house.
explanation.definitionFit: A tostada is a Mexican fried tortilla topped with beans, meat and salad, served as a dish.

clue.text: Careful wrapping of ancient wine the setter has

indicators.note: the wrapping of a parcel is on its outside, so only the outer letters of ancient count

parts.note: first and last letters
tent is a deep red Spanish wine, used for communion
the setter is I, so 'the setter has' is I'VE

explanation.surface: The setter owns some old wine and is handling its packaging with care.
explanation.definitionFit: An attentive person pays close heed to what they are doing, much like someone careful or watchful.

clue.text: Short Hobart drunk can't stand

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the remaining letters are jumbled
cut short, the place name Hobart loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone in Hobart, briefly tipsy, can no longer stay on their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' trims HOBART to HOBAR and 'drunk' rearranges it. Hobart is the capital of Tasmania; 'can't stand' looks like a drunk's wobble but means hate.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to loathe it, which is what we mean when we say we can't stand it.

clue.text: Trick expected to involve Penny

indicators.note: to involve something is to include it, so one letter goes inside the other word

parts.note: something due is expected to arrive
P is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: A con is expected to rope in someone called Penny.
explanation.definitionFit: To dupe someone is to deceive or fool them, so as a verb it matches trick.

clue.text: Important day united people inside of Italy

parts.note: MON is the short form of Monday
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names
men are people

indicators.note: the inside of a word is what remains once its first and last letters are stripped

parts.note: the letters between the outer pair

explanation.surface: A significant day brought people together across Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Monumental means of great size or significance, so it serves as a strong word for highly important.
